shipped.title: The Sundial Shadow Conspiracy
shipped.falseAssumption: The victim was murdered shortly before sunset as all household servants consistently testified.
shipped.discrimDesign: A controlled sundial shadow experiment is conducted by placing an identical watch face at the sundial under the same sunlight conditions at various times, demonstrating the precise shadow length and direction that contradicts servant testimonies and Edward’s claimed alibi, thereby proving the murder’s true timing and implicating Edward Marwood.
shipped.premise: In the isolated Marwood Manor during a drizzly early autumn afternoon, Edith Marwood is found stabbed in her private sitting room. The household staff and family provide conflicting timelines. The sundial in the garden and the stopped watch on Edith reveal a contradiction in the reported time of death. Arthur Langley investigates, unravelling a scheme that manipulated the timing of events and exploited social trust to conceal the real murderer within the family.

shipped.title: The Sundial’s Silent Verdict
shipped.deathMethod: poisoned with aconite concealed in ice cubes
shipped.falseAssumption: Lord Charles Harcourt died exactly at solar noon, as indicated by the sundial’s shadow.
shipped.discrimDesign: A controlled demonstration measures the sundial’s shadow delay under similar temperature conditions, confirming the approximately ten-minute lag caused by thermal expansion of the brass gnomon. This proves the victim’s actual time of death predates servant alibis and ledger entries, invalidating their timelines and exposing the forged evidence. Additionally, re-examination of hollow ice cubes confirms the delayed-release poison mechanism unique to the culprit’s access and knowledge.
shipped.premise: On a foggy autumn day at Harcourt Manor, Lord Charles Harcourt is found dead, apparently poisoned. Everyone believes he died at solar noon, as indicated by the sundial. However, Evelyn Harcourt discovers the sundial’s shadow was delayed due to thermal expansion of the brass gnomon, meaning he died earlier. A forged ledger and servants’ contradictory testimonies about footsteps and timing further complicate the timeline. Evelyn must unravel the temporal illusion, exposing the true time of death and revealing James Harcourt as the killer who exploited this false assumption to stage his alibi.

shipped.title: The Thermally Sealed Study: A Manor House Mystery
shipped.crimeSubtype: strangulation with cord in locked study
shipped.falseAssumption: The study door was unlocked and opened shortly after Lady Beatrice was last seen alive at early evening, so the murder must have occurred then.
shipped.discrimDesign: Recreate the thermal conditions of the study’s hearth fire with an identical brass bolt latch and mantel thermometer to demonstrate the precise forty-minute delay in bolt retraction, invalidating witness claims of the door opening at early evening and confirming the murder occurred later.
shipped.premise: On a damp autumn evening at Ellsworth Manor, Lady Beatrice Ellsworth is found strangled in her locked study. Witnesses insist the study door was unlocked soon after her last sighting, and an early timeline places the murder at early evening. However, thermal evidence of the brass bolt latch reveals a delayed unlocking mechanism, contradicting all witness claims and forcing a re-examination of the murder timeline. Inspector Edmund Hargrave unravels a complex temporal deception involving estate routines, social expectations, and physical laws to reveal the true culprit.

shipped.premise: At Wentworth Manor, Lady Beatrice Wentworth is found dead, struck by a heavy brass garden gate bolt. Witnesses unanimously claim to have seen her enter the garden grounds at noon, but physical evidence and mechanical timing contradict this. Inspector Evelyn Harcourt uncovers a deception embedded in the thermal expansion delay of the garden gate’s brass latch, exposing a false timeline created by manipulated memories and overlooked physical laws. Through careful reconstruction and social scrutiny, the truth emerges: the butler, James Porter, exploited the garden gate’s delayed bolt release to commit murder, hiding the true time of death and misdirecting suspicion.

shipped.premise: On a foggy autumn evening in 1930s Yorkshire, Lady Beatrice Langley is found dead in her chambers. Witnesses swear the manor's choir bell rang the hour after her death, suggesting a timeline that contradicts physical evidence. Inspector Gerald Havers must unravel the truth behind the acoustic deception and social tensions to reveal the murderer among family and staff.

shipped.deathMethod: struck with heavy copper sundial gnomon
shipped.falseAssumption: The victim was alive until at least twenty past ten, as indicated by the sundial’s shadow position and multiple witness sightings in the garden.

shipped.premise: On a cool autumn morning at the isolated Ellsworth Manor in Yorkshire, Lady Beatrice Ellsworth was found dead, struck by the manor's heavy copper sundial gnomon. Initial witness testimonies and the sundial's shadow suggested she was alive well into the late morning. Inspector Harold Wren's meticulous investigation reveals that thermal contraction of the sundial's copper plate shifted the shadow, misleading everyone about the time of death. This false timeline concealed the murderer’s exact opportunity. Through careful analysis of environmental clues and witness statements, Inspector Wren unravels the true sequence of events, exposing Charles Pembroke, the estate manager, who exploited the manor’s physical and social constraints to commit murder.

shipped.premise: During the village fete in Little Middleton, the respected village council chairman Reginald Hargrave is found strangled beside the sundial near the village green. The apparent time of death, indicated by the sundial's shadow, seems to place the murder at early evening during the fete's peak. However, the sundial's shadow was frozen by a thin layer of frost that formed after sunset, misleading witnesses about the true time. Eleanor Hargrave, the victim's sister and village schoolteacher, investigates the temporal illusion, uncovering a layered deception exploiting natural phenomena and village gossip. The true timeline reveals the murderer acted under cover of dense fog and social distractions, with a motive rooted in land disputes and Cold War era anxieties.

shipped.title: The Elevator Cage Enigma
shipped.location: Three-story Art Deco hotel above a rocky Atlantic shoreline
shipped.deathMethod: struck with a heavy glass decanter
shipped.falseAssumption: No one could reach Dr. Finch’s suite during the critical forty minutes, because the elevator never left the ground floor.

shipped.premise: On a foggy spring night at Pendrift Head’s Art Deco hotel, Dr. Mallory Finch is found dead in her locked third-floor suite, a shattered decanter beside her. The only access—by caged elevator—seemed impossible, as it was observed at the ground floor through the critical forty-minute window. Suspicion falls on staff, guests, and rivals alike, until Eleanor Voss unravels a spatial misdirection: the elevator’s indicator and gate were manipulated, enabling the true killer to slip past unnoticed. Physical traces and constraint logic expose Sylvia Trent, the secretary desperate to hide her forgery, as the only one with means and motive to exploit the illusion.

shipped.title: The Canary's Slippers: A Seaside Hotel Identity Mystery
shipped.deathMethod: struck on the head with a brass candlestick
shipped.falseAssumption: Captain Ivor Hale could not have committed the murder because he was seen by several witnesses on the ocean-facing veranda at ten minutes past eleven.
shipped.discrimDesign: A controlled walk is staged on the wet sand with both Captain Hale and Beatrice Quill, each wearing Hale’s slippers. The depth and pattern of Quill’s right-footed limp match exactly the suspicious footprints from the night of the murder, while Hale’s do not. Seaweed is again transferred by Quill into the service corridor, recreating the earlier physical trace. This proves Quill impersonated Hale and that only Hugo Vane could have orchestrated the timing and access.
shipped.premise: On a stormy night at the Oceanview Hotel in Sidmouth, Dr. Mallory Finch is found dead in his suite, his skull crushed by a heavy brass candlestick. Multiple guests and staff swear that the prime suspect, Captain Ivor Hale, could not have committed the crime, as he was seen on the ocean-facing veranda at the supposed time of death. Yet Eleanor Voss, observing a trail of physical clues, begins to suspect that someone exploited the hotel’s strict routines and the confusion of identity to create a nearly perfect alibi. The solution hinges on a subtle substitution: a staff member impersonated the suspect by donning his distinctive slippers and overcoat, leaving misleading traces in the freshly-wet sand outside the veranda. Only by piecing together the contradictory evidence of footprints, damp slippers, and staff access can the detective expose the real murderer and the trick that shielded him.
